I am 65 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou my whole life. I have eight mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know every inch of it. At my age, I do not gamble with new crops or fancy experiments. The wheat-maize double-cropping system has fed my family for decades, and the machinery, the seed dealers, and the grain buyers are all built around it.

My winter wheat went into the ground last October after deep ploughing and harrowing. I used an improved Jimai variety because it withstands the spring dry winds here better than the old traditional types, and it does not lodge if I manage the water right. Now that the green-up has started, I will top-dress with urea at the jointing stage and irrigate four times in total: once now to wake the crop up, again at jointing, at heading, and once more during grain filling if the May heat comes early. I will spray fungicide and insecticide twice — once now against aphids and rust, and again before heading if the weather turns humid. I expect about 500 jin per mu, give or take the weather.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will not waste a single day. I will run the rotary tiller over the stubble, spread basal fertilizer, and plant hybrid summer maize — Zhengdan or a similar hybrid that matures in 95 to 100 days before the autumn cold arrives. Hybrid seed costs more, but the yield jump is worth it. I will irrigate the maize three times: at sowing to ensure emergence, at the big trumpet stage when it is thirsty, and once during grain filling. Two pesticide sprays should handle the corn borer and any leaf spot. Rotary tillage is enough for maize; there is no time for deep ploughing between wheat harvest and maize sowing, and the wheat stubble helps keep moisture in.

I have thought about growing garlic or vegetables on a patch because the prices can be high, but at my age I cannot handle the extra labor and market risk. My back is not what it used to be, and my son works in Handan city. Wheat and maize give me stable grain coupons and cash income without requiring me to haggle at the vegetable market. I also keep my soil in balance this way — the wheat straw goes back to the field, and the maize roots break up any compaction from the harvester. This is the plan I trust.
